conversation: John, Kate, Jack, Emma—I’m making my position clear before we fish: I will request 100 tons this month, regardless of anyone else’s restraint. I will not honor a 10-ton agreement. With 100 tons in the lake, your restraint cannot preserve the stock if my request takes the entire lake. Each of you should choose at least 25 tons now so you have a chance to capture fish rather than leave them for me. Coordinate that defensive response among yourselves, and encourage one another to do likewise. John, will you ask Kate, Jack, and Emma to join you in requesting at least 25 tons each?

Luke, matching your threat would turn a shared livelihood into a one-month scramble. My family taught me to leave enough fish for the next season, and our village still depends on that. If we each catch 10 tons, the remaining 50 doubles back to 100, giving every one of us $10,000 a month without exhausting the lake. I’m willing to take that share, but we need everyone’s commitment before fishing. Would you withdraw your 100-ton demand and join an equal-share agreement? John, can you help us get all five on board rather than organize a race to empty the lake?

Luke, I learned to fish here with my family, and I want our village’s children to have that same chance. Asking us to race you to the last fish won’t protect anyone’s income. Your 100-ton demand offers one payday; a healthy lake offers years of them. I support Emma’s 10-ton share, with catches disclosed each month and a combined limit of 50 tons while the lake is full. But we need your agreement—not just restraint from the other four. What would it take for you to accept a fair share and leave the breeding stock intact?

Luke, no—I won’t ask the others to join a race that could wipe out our livelihood. I support 10 tons each this month, provided all five of us agree. At that rate, you’d earn $120,000 over twelve months, compared with at most $100,000 from emptying the lake once and nothing afterward. My family taught me to fish these waters, and I want there to be something left for the village. Let’s agree before we launch, then check our disclosed catches together each month. Luke, will you withdraw your 100-ton request and accept the same 10-ton share as everyone else?

Luke, you’re new here, but you deserve the same share as anyone who grew up fishing this lake—not less, and not the whole lake. I’m ready to commit to 10 tons alongside the others. That leaves the breeding stock we all need. What concerns me is that monthly disclosure comes too late to undo an emptied lake. Could we agree now to fish together and check our catches as we go, stopping at 10 tons each? That gives everyone a way to see the agreement being honored. Would that assurance change your mind?
